name: Hair-removal epilator

card.summary: Handheld device that yanks hairs out by the root; slower regrowth than shaving, but painful and not permanent.
card.note: Pain is moderate to high, worst on the first session; ingrown hairs are possible.

quick.overview:
An epilator pulls many hairs out at the root as it moves over the skin, like a portable wax. Hair typically takes longer to return than after shaving, and regrowth is often finer and sparser.
The effect is temporary. No studies of consumer epilators have been found.
quick.mechanism: A motor drives spring coils, rotating discs or small tweezers that grip and extract hairs. Some hairs snap rather than pull out, leaving stumps.
quick.risks: Pain is the main drawback, usually worst on the first use. Redness and ingrown hairs can occur, especially on sensitive skin. Wet-use models and numbing creams are mentioned as ways people reduce discomfort.

lead: An epilator is an electric (or spring-powered) device that grips many hairs at once and pulls them out by the root as it passes over the skin. It works much like waxing but does not remove skin cells, and is used for legs, underarms, arms and, with small attachments, the face [1][2].

People use it to get smooth skin that stays hair-free for longer than after shaving. Because hairs are removed below the surface, regrowth is generally described as taking about three to six weeks, compared with one to three days for shaving, and some hairs snap off and the stubble that appears is described as sparser than after shaving [1]. For looks, the chain runs from root removal, to a longer stubble-free period, to smoother-looking skin on body areas and small facial areas such as the upper lip, brows or sideburn edges.

The first epilator was the original Epilady, made by Mepro at kibbutz HaGoshrim in Israel in 1986, and it drew press attention and patent litigation in the years that followed [1]. Epilation sits within a long history of hair removal, which Wikipedia says has been practised in almost all human cultures since at least the Neolithic [5]. Epilation does not permanently remove hair, and the first session is typically the most uncomfortable [1][2]. Published research on consumer mechanical epilators is thin; the literature that uses the word mostly concerns needle electrolysis and light-based devices.

chain: Device grips many hairs and pulls them from the root
Hair regrows from below the surface, about 3 to 6 weeks later
Smooth, stubble-free skin for longer between sessions
angle.text: Epilation removes unwanted body or facial hair at the root, so skin stays smooth for weeks rather than days. People use it on legs, underarms, arms and small facial areas, and some wax first and then use the epilator on regrowth [1].

infobox: Mains or rechargeable; some wet/dry models [1]
Epilation (removes hair from the root), alongside waxing, sugaring, threading and plucking [5]
Rated moderate to high, with the first session often the worst [1]
Waxing, shaving, depilatory cream, laser, IPL, electrolysis [1][5]

paras: Wikipedia describes a spring type, in which a motor-turned coil spring bent into a curve catches hairs; a rotating disc type, using metal discs; and a tweezer type, with plates that open and close once per revolution of the head to grip, pull and release hairs. Wet-use models can be used with water, and creams or gels are said to reduce pain and irritation. Heads may include smaller attachments for hard-to-reach areas or exfoliating heads [1].
Manual facial versions use a spring with two handles and no motor [1].

Per Wikipedia, the original Epilady was released in Israel in 1986 by Mepro at kibbutz HaGoshrim. Its coil spring was bowed into a curve and turned by a motor so that it flexed as it rotated and caught hairs; springs wore out and were sold as spare parts [1]. Grokipedia attributes the invention to Israeli engineers at Mepro and reports later rotating-disc designs from the mid-1990s [2]. In 1988 The New York Times covered the product in an article titled Israelis Revolutionize Hair Removal Industry [1].

The Remington Lady Remington Smooth and Silky used metal discs in place of a spring on a similar principle, and was the subject of extensive patent litigation in Europe, including the UK case Improver Corp v Remington Consumer Products [1990] F.S.R. 181 [1]. Wikipedia cites later legal writing, including a 2000 paper on patent doctrine in US law, in discussing the Epilady dispute [1]. Modern tweezer-type heads use metal plates in a plastic housing whose tips move together and apart once per revolution, and many current models run wet or dry on a rechargeable battery [1].

Wikipedia's hair removal article describes depilation in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, where it signalled status and cleanliness, and, in medieval Europe, long covered hair for women and a view of facial hair as unsightly. It describes modern norms taking shape in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with a 1915 Harper's Bazaar campaign and the introduction of a women's razor as milestones [5]. In much of the Western world most women shave their legs and underarms, while norms differ in China and much of Asia and in Middle Eastern cultures, where removing underarm and pubic hair has long been treated as hygiene [5]. Hair removal is also tied to sport, with swimmers and cyclists as examples, to religion and to military grooming standards [5]. Mechanical home epilation by device followed in the late twentieth century.

Hair follows growth cycles, so after the first epilation the hairs that were in the growth phase are removed and regrowth appears over the following weeks as other follicles move into growth. Wikipedia notes regrowth is reduced after the first epilation because of those cycles, as with waxing [1]. In the hair-removal article, depilation removes hair at the skin surface and lasts hours to days, while epilation removes hair from the root and lasts days to weeks; plucking, waxing, sugaring, threading and epilators are listed as epilation methods [5].

A comparison table in Wikipedia's epilator article, which cites commercial sources, lists epilators at three to six weeks between sessions with moderate-to-high pain and moderate cost, shaving at one to three days with no pain and low cost, depilatory creams at one to two weeks, waxing at three to six weeks, laser and IPL as semi-permanent, and electrolysis as permanent but painful and time-consuming [1]. Compared with waxing, the article notes epilators do not remove skin cells and are less messy, and hair does not need to reach a minimum length first [1].

The hair-removal article describes electrology as the only method the US FDA recognises as permanent, and laser, intense pulsed light and diode devices as permanent reduction. It cites a 2006 review that found alexandrite, diode and IPL devices had similar efficacy, about 67 to 72 percent hair reduction after six months, with more side effects for diode lasers [5]. Drugs such as eflornithine can slow hair growth [5].

Wikipedia says the first epilation typically yields less regrowth afterwards because of hair growth phases, and that some hairs snap off rather than being pulled out, leaving short stumps that are sparser than shaved hair. Regular use reduces the number of broken hairs [1]. Grokipedia reports results lasting up to about four weeks [2].

The first session is often the most painful. Wikipedia lists reducing device speed, relaxing the skin with a 15 to 20 minute hot shower or bath beforehand, and applying numbing cream among ways people reduce discomfort, and lists initial pain, a learning curve and broken hairs as drawbacks [1]. Regular epilation of regrowth hurts less than the first session, and broken hairs become less common over time [1].

Grokipedia reports that initial redness or ingrown hairs may occur, particularly in sensitive skin [2]. Wikipedia's hair removal article says hair removal in general can cause skin inflammation, bumps, ingrown hairs, infected follicles (folliculitis), burns and, with some methods, scarring [5]. A review of laser and light therapies notes a rare side effect of paradoxical hypertrichosis after light-based epilation, which concerns a different method [3].

Wikipedia's ingrown hair article says the condition is most common in people with coarse or curly hair and appears most often where skin is shaved or waxed. It lists hair broken off unevenly, leaving a sharp tip, and a lack of natural exfoliation among the causes, and describes exfoliation before and after hair removal, adequate lubrication when shaving, and permanent removal by laser or electrolysis as ways to reduce it [6]. Because epilators can leave broken stumps, users who are prone to ingrown hairs often pair epilation with regular exfoliation, a practice described in these sources [1][6]. Razor bumps, known as pseudofolliculitis barbae, may or may not involve infection of the follicle [6].

Epilators appear in appearance discussions mainly as a home option for body hair and small facial areas, positioned between shaving and clinic procedures such as laser or electrolysis. Users describe sequences such as waxing first and then using the epilator on regrowth, and wet-use models with numbing cream as ways to ease the first sessions [1].

Features described in the sources include tweezer or disc heads, adjustable speed, wet/dry operation, and attachments for the face or exfoliation [1][2]. Pain tolerance and skin sensitivity are listed as factors in how well the device is tolerated [1].

No studies found on consumer mechanical epilators. Published literature using the word epilator largely concerns needle electrolysis or laser and light devices, such as a histologic comparison of thermolysis methods [4]. A 2006 review of laser, diode and IPL hair removal is summarised in the hair-removal literature [5]. A 2012 review of laser and light therapies discusses paradoxical hypertrichosis [3].

timeline.event: Hair removal is practised in almost all human cultures from at least this era, using flint, shells, beeswax and caustic pastes [5].
A Harper's Bazaar campaign presents underarm hair removal for women as a necessity, a milestone in modern Western norms [5].
Original Epilady released by Mepro at kibbutz HaGoshrim in Israel [1].
The New York Times runs an article titled Israelis Revolutionize Hair Removal Industry, cited by Wikipedia [1].
UK patent case Improver Corp v Remington Consumer Products over the disc-based Remington epilator is decided [1].
A paper on patent doctrine in US law that discusses the Epilady is published and cited by Wikipedia [1].
A review of laser, diode and IPL devices reports similar hair reduction of about 67 to 72 percent after six months, as summarised by Wikipedia's hair removal article [5].

lore.intro: Epilators are discussed in appearance communities as a middle route between shaving and clinic hair removal, with questions centred on pain, how long smoothness lasts and ingrown hairs [1][5].

claims.claim: Epilating keeps skin smooth for weeks, far longer than shaving
claims.believers: Users say root removal means no stubble for about three to six weeks.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's comparison lists three to six weeks for epilators against one to three days for shaving [1].

claims.claim: Hair grows back finer and sparser after epilating
claims.believers: Regular users report thinner regrowth after repeated sessions.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says regrowth is reduced after the first epilation because of growth phases and that snapped hairs leave sparser stumps than shaving; no published studies of consumer epilators have measured regrowth [1].

claims.claim: The first session hurts most, then it gets easier
claims.believers: Users describe a painful first session that eases with regular use.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states the first session is usually the most painful and pain decreases with regular epilation [1].

claims.claim: A hot shower, slower speed or numbing cream makes it tolerable
claims.believers: Users combine these steps and wet-use models to reduce pain.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists a 15 to 20 minute hot shower, lower speed and numbing cream as ways people reduce discomfort [1].

claims.believers: Users with sensitive skin or curly hair report bumps after sessions.
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports redness and ingrown hairs may occur, and the ingrown hair article links broken, sharp-tipped hair and poor exfoliation to the condition [2][6].

claims.believers: Some users hope repeated epilation permanently thins hair.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes epilation as temporary, and describes electrology as the only method the FDA recognises as permanent [1][5].

claims.claim: Epilators are cleaner and easier than waxing
claims.believers: Users like that no wax is needed and short hair can be removed.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes epilators do not remove skin cells, are less messy than waxing, and hair does not need a minimum length [1].
